name: Triad Traverse (West-to-East Ridge Traverse)
beta: Climbed by Sam Boyce and Kyle Willis in July 2018 as part of a four-day 'Boston Marathon' link-up; they knew of no previously published complete west-to-east crossing. From Sibley Pass, a faint climbers' trail (generally used to access Marble Creek Basin) leads along the ridge; the route then tags West, Middle, and East Triad in sequence along the crest. The west face of Middle Triad has the best rock on the route and holds the technical crux at 5.6 R; elsewhere the ridge is serious, exposed 4th-class and low-5th-class scrambling on generally poor ('choss') rock. A separate 2018 descent of the East Ridge toward the Eldorado Glacier involved pushing past large loose blocks and roughly 500 ft of very exposed 5.6–5.7 downclimbing to reach the glacier.
overview: A long, loose ridge traverse across all three of The Triad's summits (West, Middle, East), with sustained exposed 4th-class and low-5th-class scrambling and a 5.6 R crux pitch on Middle Triad's west face — among the least-documented lines in the Boston Basin/Eldorado group.

current.approach: Same trailhead and initial approach as the East Peak standard route: Hidden Lake Trailhead via Cascade River Road and FSR 1540, then Hidden Lake Trail #745 to Sibley Pass (~6,040–6,060 ft). From the pass, rather than dropping toward Hidden Lake Basin, follow the ridge crest and the faint climbers' trail east toward West Triad.
current.descent: Parties descending off the Triad ridge toward the Eldorado Glacier have reported pushing past refrigerator- to car-sized loose blocks and down-climbing roughly 500 ft of exposed 5.6–5.7 terrain to reach the glacier — one party called it among the boldest down-climbing they had committed to. This descent should be treated as seriously as the traverse itself; carrying a rope and a small rack for short lowers is prudent even though no fixed rappel line is established.
current.detailed_rack: A rack suited to 5.6 R climbing (small-to-medium cams and nuts) plus a rope for the crux pitch and any short lowers on the loose descent toward the Eldorado Glacier.
current.pro_needs: The 5.6 R crux and much of the ridge offer limited or run-out protection — treat gear as supplemental to careful, deliberate movement rather than a guarantee.

name: The West Face
beta: Shares its first pitch with the Northwest Corner up a dirty face/chimney to a huge sandy ledge, then follows a steep right-facing corner, a lieback flake with an airy step past a bolt, and a sustained undercling/lieback corner crack into the crux: a thin tips crack that eases into easier ground higher up, finishing on lower-angle crack and slab climbing.
overview: The West Face (III 5.11-) is a 6-pitch, roughly 500 ft (152 m) route first climbed (with aid) by Fred Beckey and Dave Beckstad in 1965, with Steve Risse and Dave Tower making the first free ascent in 1985.

current.approach: From the Blue Lake Trailhead (5,400 ft), follow the Blue Lake Trail about 1.5 miles to the climbers' path, leave the trail into the basin below the Liberty Bell Group, pass South Early Winters Spire, and traverse left along the base to the shared start with the Northwest Corner. Allow 1-2 hours car-to-base.
approach_variant_names: Blue Lake Trail into the basin, past South Early Winters Spire, then left along the base
current.descent: Two descent options exist. The original line drops down the left side through a notch with three single-rope rappels, includes one free-hanging rappel over a chockstone, and finishes with some scrambling back to the base. The bolted alternative - six bolted rap stations starting about 15 feet right of where the finishing cracks top out - is generally considered faster and less committing.
current.detailed_rack: Doubles from fingers (0.1in) to 3in; consider triples in the tips/fingers range if climbing near your limit, given the sustained thin crux pitch.
rack: Cams, doubles fingers to 3" (triples in tips/finger sizes recommended near your limit)
Small wires/stoppers for the crux and upper pitches
4 long slings (60cm/120cm) for anchors and awkward gear
current.pro_needs: Well protected on gear throughout, including the crux tips crack, but the small sizes see heavy use - don't skimp on tiny cams.
current.rope_note: Published descriptions do not state rope length explicitly; ~710ft across 6 pitches makes 70m practical for full pitch lengths. Original descent: 3 single-rope raps into the North/South spire notch, one free-hanging rap off a large chockstone, then a short tree rap or downclimb.

name: North Peak
beta: Parties typically combine this with the South Peak lookout climb in a single trip since both share the same long approach. From Camp Saddle/Tin Can Gap, descend onto the glacier and traverse to the base of the North Peak, then climb the West Couloir to the South Face. One party describes the climbing as Class 4 with one Class 5 move in the chimney, then easing to Class 2 and 3 near the summit — easier than it is sometimes described, with rock character compared to Chimney Rock.
overview: Contrary to this route's name, the historic Three Fingers fire lookout actually sits on the South Peak, not here — the North Peak is a separate, harder objective and is widely considered (though not unanimously, per conflicting elevation surveys) the true high point of the mountain. There is no maintained trail, no ladders, and no register cabin; it's a roped alpine scramble/climb reached via glacier travel from Goat Flats and Tin Can Gap, with genuine exposure and no easy bail once committed to the upper chimney.

current.approach: FR 41 is closed to vehicles at the Canyon Creek bridge, so first walk or bike roughly 8-9 miles of road to the trailhead. The climb starts at the Tupso Pass trailhead on the Three Fingers-Goat Flats-Saddle Lake Trail #641. The trail climbs through forest, crossing a couple of small seasonal streams, to Saddle Lake at about 2.5 miles (last reliable, easy water before the alpine section; no camping within 200 ft of the lake and no fires from here on). From Saddle Lake continue roughly 2–2.5 more miles, gaining out of the timber into the open meadows of Goat Flats (~4.5 mi from the TH) — good camps and the last easy tentsites with views to Puget Sound. From Goat Flats the trail contours and climbs about 2 more miles to Tin Can Gap (~6.2 mi, roughly 3,500-3,800 ft of the day's gain done); this is the last maintained-trail point and the standard high camp/bivy for peak days. Tin Can Gap gives the first real view of the three summits and the Queest-Alb (Three Fingers) Glacier below. From the gap the route drops about 400 ft off-trail down snow/talus onto the glacier — early season this is a straightforward snow descent, but by late summer expect bare ice and a moat between rock and ice that requires care (crampons/axe recommended into at least July); crevasses open on the glacier by mid-summer so rope up if traveling as a team when covered. Cross the glacier and climb back up roughly 1,000 ft on the far side to the col between Middle and North Peak — this climb is on a mix of snow/scree and low-angle rock and is the route-finding crux of the approach. From the col, the North Peak route follows a ramp leading left then angling right into a shallow chimney, with sustained 4th-class and a few low-5th-class (5.0-5.4) exposed moves through loose-to-fair rock to the summit block; a harder 5.4 line exists on the upper west face but is avoided by most parties for rock quality. Carry a rope, a small rack, and glacier gear (axe/crampons, and a rope+harness for crevasse hazard) even in a scramble-grade season. Water at Saddle Lake is poor; a better stream runs about halfway from there to Goat Flats, and melt streams are good beyond Tin Can Gap in late summer.
approach_variant_names: Trail #641 from Tupso Pass over Goat Flats and Tin Can Gap
current.descent: Reverse the ascent line off the North Peak summit. Parties describe two to three rappels getting back down through the 4th/low-5th-class chimney-and-ramp section to easier 3rd-class ground above the glacier — plan on a single 60m rope (or two ropes if parties want to link stations in fewer pulls). The first rappel station is commonly an old fixed sling/tat anchor left by previous parties, but it should not be trusted blindly — inspect it or back it up, and be prepared to build natural gear anchors (cams/nuts on horns or cracks) for the remaining stations since fixed gear is inconsistent year to year. After the rappels, downclimb/scramble the remaining 3rd-class terrain back to the col, reverse the ~1,000 ft descent to the glacier, re-cross the Queest-Alb Glacier (watch the moat and any crevasses), climb back up to Tin Can Gap, and reverse Trail #641 through Goat Flats and Saddle Lake to the trailhead. Rockfall in the chimney/gully and a icy glacier moat are the main descent-specific hazards; a mid-to-late-season descent in soft/rotten snow on the glacier headwall can also be tricky.
current.detailed_rack: A light rack — slings and a small selection of cams/nuts — is enough for protecting the short 5th-class chimney move; the rest of the route is unroped scrambling.
rack: Small rack: slings, small cams/nuts for the chimney
current.pro_needs: Minimal gear placements needed, concentrated at the one 5th-class chimney move; considerable exposure on this section warrants a rope even though the technical difficulty is modest.
current.rope_note: Standard route crosses the Queest-Alb glacier before a rocky scramble and three fixed wooden ladders leading to the lookout on the south peak. Ice axe/crampons required whenever the glacier headwall/steep snow slope below the summit is present.

name: Middle Peak (South Face)
beta: The Middle Peak is climbed far less often than the South Peak (lookout) or North Peak and has very little published route detail; it shares the same long Goat Flats/Tin Can Gap approach as the other two summits before diverging toward the Middle Peak's south side. Treat any attempt as a serious, lightly-documented alpine rock objective and be prepared to route-find.
overview: The middle of the three summits and the harder of the trio to reach, Middle Peak is typically climbed from a glacier camp near the col between it and the North Peak rather than as a standalone 'south face' outing — most parties combine it with the North Peak in a two- or three-summit push. It sees far less traffic than the ladder-and-lookout South Peak.

current.approach: FR 41 is closed to vehicles at the Canyon Creek bridge, so first walk or bike roughly 8-9 miles of road to the trailhead. Then follow the same approach as the other two summits: Trail #641 from Tupso Pass over Saddle Lake (2.5 mi) and Goat Flats (~4.5 mi) to Tin Can Gap (~6.2-7 mi), then drop ~400 ft off-trail onto the Queest-Alb Glacier and cross it (moat and possible crevasse hazard — crampons/axe recommended, rope up if crevasses are open). Most parties bivy on or near the glacier below the peaks rather than pushing all three summits car-to-car. From a glacier-side camp, Middle Peak's south face is reached by a short climb/traverse toward the base of the peak; one detailed trip report logged the summit in about 37 minutes from a glacier bivy. The route itself is solid 3rd- and 4th-class scrambling on the lower face, transitioning to looser, more broken 3rd-class rock higher up — take care with rockfall onto anyone below, and expect the climbing to run longer than the peak's modest height suggests since the face is broader than it looks from the glacier. No technical rock gear is required for the standard line, but a rope is worth carrying for the optional short rappel on descent (see below) and in case conditions call for a belay on the looser upper section. Water at Saddle Lake is poor; a better stream runs about halfway from there to Goat Flats, and melt streams are good beyond Tin Can Gap in late summer.
approach_variant_names: Trail #641 to Tin Can Gap, then a glacier-side camp
current.descent: Middle Peak is primarily downclimbed by reversing the ascent line — most parties report no fixed rappel is needed, picking a careful line down through the looser upper 3rd class rock and the sounder 3rd/4th class below. Some parties do choose a short single-rope rappel (natural anchor — a horn, block, or sling around a chockstone/tree; no bolted anchors reported) to bypass the loosest or most exposed step on the upper face, particularly with larger groups or when downclimbing feels riskier than descending on the rope; a single 30m or half a 60m rope is plenty for this. After regaining the glacier-side camp/route, reverse the glacier crossing (mind the moat), climb back to Tin Can Gap, and follow Trail #641 out via Goat Flats and Saddle Lake. Loose rock on the upper face is the main descent hazard — helmet strongly recommended — along with the same glacier moat/crevasse considerations shared with the other two summits.
current.detailed_rack: Small rack/slings for the short exposed steps
current.pro_needs: Minimal pro for the harder moves

name: South Peak via Lookout
beta: This is the line Harry Bedal, Harold Engles, and Frank Benesh used to reach the South Peak summit to build the fire lookout in the early 1930s, and it remains the standard way up. From the trailhead the route follows trail to Saddle Lake, Goat Flats, and Tin Can Gap, then crosses the edge of the Queest-Alb Glacier before a rock scramble and a set of three fixed ladders (rebar and timber anchored into steep rock) gain the summit block and lookout. It is popular as a long day trip or, more commonly, an overnight from Goat Flats or Tin Can Gap given the approach length.
overview: A long, storied outing to the historic fire lookout perched on the South Peak of Three Fingers, crossing the Queest-Alb Glacier. The L-4 gable lookout was built 1930-1932 by Darrington-area mountaineers Harold Engles and Frank Benesh (with Harry Bedal having assisted in the 1929 feasibility scout), staffed seasonally from 1933 through 1942, later rebuilt by volunteers, and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1987 — roughly the top 15 feet of the summit block was blasted flat to seat the cabin. It remains one of the most iconic hike-scrambles in the Cascade foothills, thanks largely to the three vertical ladders cabled to the final summit tower.

current.approach: FR 41 is closed to vehicles at the Canyon Creek bridge, so first walk or bike roughly 8-9 miles of road to the trailhead. From the Tupso Pass trailhead, follow Three Fingers Trail #641 through forest to Saddle Lake (~2.5 mi, last easy water — no fires or camping within 200 ft of the lake past this point), then continue up through meadows to Goat Flats (~4.5 mi total), a broad subalpine bench with the best camping on the route and views out to Puget Sound. From Goat Flats the trail climbs roughly 2 more miles to Tin Can Gap (~6.2-7 mi total, most of the day's 4,200 ft gain banked); this is where the maintained trail effectively ends and most casual hikers turn around. Beyond the gap, drop off-trail onto the Queest-Alb (Three Fingers) Glacier — a short but real glacier crossing with a moat between ice and rock that widens through the season (crampons/axe strongly recommended, especially before August); a rope is worth carrying if crevasses are open. On the far side, scramble up rock and snow past the base of the summit block to the historic lookout's ladder system: three fixed wooden ladders bolted/pinned into the rock, stacked in sequence, gaining the final class-5-equivalent rock band to the lookout deck. The transition between the second and third ladder is the trickiest move and is awkward with a full pack; exposure is significant and a slip here would be serious, so this last pitch is why the route is rated a scramble rather than a hike despite no rope typically being used. Some parties fix or find a hand-line/rope on a short exposed rock step just past Tin Can Gap before the glacier — treat it as unverified fixed gear.
approach_variant_names: Tupso Pass trailhead, Trail #641 (road drivable)
Road-closure variation — walk or bike FR 41
current.descent: This is a walk-off/downclimb route with no roped rappelling on the standard line. Downclimb the three fixed ladders in reverse (facing in, one at a time, mind the awkward 2nd-to-3rd ladder transition), then reverse the rock/snow scramble back down to and across the Queest-Alb Glacier, watching the moat and any open crevasses. Climb back up to Tin Can Gap and reverse Trail #641 through Goat Flats and Saddle Lake to the trailhead. The main descent hazards are the exposed ladder pitch (a fall here would be very serious despite no technical rappelling), a soft or icy glacier moat later in the day, and lingering steep snow on the south ridge in early season — an ice axe is recommended into mid-summer. No rappel gear is needed for the standard route.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier travel gear; rope for the glacier and exposed ladder/scramble section.
current.pro_needs: Minimal; primarily snow/glacier protection.

name: Middle Peak via South Face - South Chimney
beta: From the Mineral Creek Trailhead, the route follows the Mineral Creek trail before heading off-trail through brush to the base of a long talus slope on Middle Peak's south side. The talus steepens toward the Main-Middle notch, which is marked by a chockstone; from there the line traverses a broad south-facing ledge to a rock gable roughly 150 ft below the summit, then climbs a solid, enjoyable class 4 chimney directly to the top.
overview: A distinct line up Three Queens' Middle Peak (6,600 ft), climbing the south face to a rock gable below the summit and finishing up a class 4 chimney system; it has been climbed solo, car-to-car, as a day scramble/climb.

current.approach: Same trailhead and initial trail as the East/Main Peak standard route: Mineral Creek Trailhead (2,400 ft), across the Kachess River ford, 1.7 miles of trail to the Mineral Creek crossing, then about 1 mile through vine maple brush to the base of the south-side talus slope below Middle Peak. As of late May 2026 a gate stands near the old trailhead and the trail now starts from a small lot (4-5 cars) at the end of a narrow logging road; a short descent leads to the first log crossing. The Kachess River and Mineral Creek are both crossed on logs in June and July; the logs are bare and slick, so some parties sit and shuffle across.
approach_variant_names: Mineral Creek Trail, then off-trail through the vine maple to the south-side talus
current.descent: From the summit, set up two sequential 60-ft (18m) rappels down the South Chimney to regain the south-facing ledge below the rock gable. From there, downclimb/traverse back toward the Main-Middle notch area and descend the talus slope, retracing the brushy off-trail section and the Mineral Creek trail back to the trailhead and river ford.
current.detailed_rack: A single rope (60m or two ropes for the raps) plus rappel/anchor-building gear (webbing/cord for a chockstone or block anchor, rappel device) — no fixed anchors are documented on this route. A small rack of slings for natural pro on the chimney is reasonable.
current.pro_needs: Anchor-building material (webbing/cordelette) for two 60-ft rappel stations off natural features in the chimney; no cams/nuts specifically documented as needed.

name: Standard Scramble
beta: From the Mineral Creek Trail, leave the tread west of the broad waterfall gully and climb off-trail through vine maple and then long south-side talus and scree to the southeast shoulder (about 6,200 ft). From the shoulder, traverse roughly a quarter mile of steep snow or talus onto the northeast ridge, then scramble the final ~400 ft up the ridge to the East (true) summit. The step onto the ridge and the upper ridge are loose, exposed class 3 with a short class 4 move or two, so test every hold. A separate, longer line from a camp at Upper Park Lake climbs the north side to the Main-Middle notch and crosses a ledge system on the north face; it is a different route, not part of this one.
overview: Three Queens is a triple-summited peak on Chikamin Ridge in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, the second-highest point on the ridge after Chikamin Peak (6,994 ft). The East Peak (6,693 ft) is the true summit; the Middle (~6,600 ft) and West (~6,400 ft) peaks are linked to it by a narrow, exposed connecting ridge that includes a Class 5 knife-edge section most parties avoid via a ledge traverse. The mountain sits almost directly north of Little Kachess Lake, between Mineral Creek (south/southwest) and the Cooper River (north/east). First climbed in 1925 by a Mountaineers party led by Glen Bremerman and C.A. Fisher; the name was adopted by the USBGN in 1940. The Pacific Crest Trail crosses the peak's west slope en route between Spectacle Lake and Chikamin Ridge, though the summit scramble itself leaves the PCT/approach trail well below treeline.

current.approach: Trailhead: Mineral Creek Trailhead (Trail #1331), roughly 2,360-2,400 ft, reached via FR-4600 over Cooper Pass. From the parking area the trail promptly crosses the Kachess River — look for logs spanning it; when they're not in place it's a short, easy wade. The trail then climbs gently north through second-growth and brushy old avalanche paths, muddy in spots with the occasional blowdown to step over. At about 1.6-1.7 miles it crosses Mineral Creek itself; this crossing carries enough current in early season that parties often lay a short log/rock crossing rather than ford, and the ruins of an old mine and mill sit just off-trail here as a landmark (and a fine last water source). Continue upstream through brushy trail for roughly another mile, to about the 2.7-mile mark, watching on the right (west) for a break in the timber around 3,300-3,500 ft — this is where an obvious boot/social path leaves the maintained trail and cuts west through 100-200 ft of vine-maple brush to reach the base of Three Queens' south-face talus. Leave the trail west of the broad waterfall gully that drains the south face (not the drainage directly above the creek crossing) — trip reports flag this junction as easy to get wrong in the brush. From here it's off-trail talus and scree for the remaining 1,400-1,700 ft of gain: the lower ~1,000 ft is moderately angled, largely stable large talus; above that the rock turns smaller and looser, funneling into choss gullies that run generally class 2 with short class 3 sections higher up. A snow ramp (commonly encountered around 5,200 ft) can persist into midsummer on some lines, so carry an ice axe for early-season attempts. Loose rock and rockfall are the dominant hazards through the upper talus and gullies — wear a helmet and keep the group tight so climbers aren't stacked below one another. The final ~400 ft to the 6,693-ft high point is the most exposed scrambling on the route, with brief but genuine class 3 moves and blocks that can shift underfoot; published descriptions of this section as 'class 3' are considered generous by several parties who found it heads-up the whole way.
approach_variant_names: Mineral Creek Trail to the break in the timber west of the waterfall gully
current.descent: The standard descent reverses the ascent line: back down the summit scrambling, through the upper choss gullies, down the talus to the vine-maple break, and out the 2.7-2.8 miles of trail to the Mineral Creek Trailhead. No rappelling is required on this walk-off/downclimb line (rappels: 0), but the loose upper talus and gullies are generally regarded as more hazardous descending than climbing — face in through the class 3 sections, move deliberately on the small unstable talus, and regroup below rockfall lines rather than descending stacked up. Any snow ramp encountered on the ascent is often the fastest way down (plunge-step or glissade with an axe). Total time from summit to car is commonly reported around 3.5-4 hours. Note: if a party instead climbs the optional South Chimney variant (class 4, on the south face) rather than the standard talus/gully line, that route does NOT walk off — the chimney itself is descended by rappel: two rappels of about 60 ft each, reported consistently in trip logs. Anchors are natural (chockstones, horns, or slung blocks), as this is unbolted alpine rock, so carry cord/webbing to build or back up anchors. A single 60m rope handles both rappels doubled; two shorter ropes joined also work. Below the chimney, the descent rejoins the same long talus and scree slopes and the trail out. Hazards specific to this variant are loose rock in the chimney and rope-snag risk against the blocky walls.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack.
current.pro_needs: None.

name: West Peak via West Ridge - West Face
beta: After camping at Spectacle Point (5,800 ft), the route climbs the West Ridge and West Face of West Peak to the summit — a mix of rock scrambling and rock climbing, i.e. class 3-4 terrain without a documented technical crux comparable to the Middle Peak chimney.
overview: A rock scramble/climb up Three Queens' West Peak (6,400 ft) via its West Ridge and West Face, approached from a high camp at Spectacle Point after a multi-day hike in via Mineral Creek and Park Lakes.

current.approach: From the Mineral Creek Trailhead (2,400 ft), follow the Kachess River/Mineral Creek approach through Park Lakes to Spectacle Point (5,800 ft) — a longer multi-day approach (16 miles round trip in the accounts report) than the Middle Peak day-route.
current.descent: Descend the West Ridge/West Face by the ascent line back to Spectacle Point, then follow the Park Lakes-Mineral Creek trail back out to the Mineral Creek Trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is documented for this line beyond what a party would carry for general class 3-4 scrambling; no roped pitches or fixed protection are recorded.

name: Southeast Ridge
beta: From the Yellow Aster Butte/Tomyhoi Lake Trailhead, follow maintained trail up to the high meadows and tarns below Yellow Aster Butte (~5,580 ft), then leave the trail and head NNW over a hump to a col (~6,266 ft). Climb the broadening ridge (Tomyhoi Arm); where it narrows, bypass on broad benches on the north side, then traverse the top of the Tomyhoi Glacier to avoid rock pinnacles lower on the ridge. Cross a moat/notch below the final summit pyramid (hard snow, ice axe useful) and finish with a delightful but exposed Class 3 scramble on solid rock to the true summit; one party describes a V-shaped Class 3.5 slot near the top that some parties belay or lower packs through, especially on descent.
overview: Tomyhoi Peak (7,439 ft) is the high point of a long summit ridge in the Skagit Range of the North Cascades, rising immediately south of the Canada–U.S. border within the Mount Baker Wilderness. Its summit sits over 4,400 ft above Damfino Creek in barely a mile — some of the sharpest local relief in the range — and a small unofficial glacier clings to its north side. From the top, sightlines run north to Mount Larrabee (its taller parent peak) and the American and Canadian Border Peaks, and south to Mount Shuksan and Mount Baker. First climbed by Lage Wernstedt in 1927, the peak is now most often reached via the long Southeast Ridge from the Yellow Aster Butte basin — a popular scramble that trades technical difficulty for a genuinely wild, alpine feel and real route-finding through a string of rock gendarmes.

current.approach: From the Yellow Aster Butte/Tomyhoi Lake trailhead (~3,600-3,700 ft) on Twin Lakes Road (FR 3065), start on the well-maintained Yellow Aster Butte Trail (Trail #686). The trail climbs through forest switchbacks and crosses a couple of small seasonal creeks/seep crossings in the first mile — reliable water here early season, less so by late summer. At roughly 1.5 miles you reach the signed junction with the Tomyhoi Lake Trail, which splits off to the right toward Gold Run Pass (~5,400 ft); stay left on the Yellow Aster Butte Trail. Beyond the junction the trail contours into the Yellow Aster Meadows and a basin of small tarns/lakes at about 5,200-5,600 ft (roughly 2 hours/4 miles from the car at a moderate pace) — this is the last dependable water on route. From the basin, leave the maintained trail and head north/NNW over a broad hump and down to a col around 6,266 ft, then pick up a well-defined, boot-packed climbers' path along the crest of the Tomyhoi Arm ridge. As the ridge narrows above roughly 6,800-7,000 ft, bypass the narrowest sections on broad benches on the north (right) side rather than staying on the crest. The path eventually fades into scree and talus as you approach the toe of the Tomyhoi Glacier; traverse along the top edge of the glacier (minor crevasse hazard depending on year/season — assess before committing) to avoid several rock pinnacles, aiming for a notch/moat below the false summit at about 7,250 ft. This upper section is loose, exposed, and route-finding is not obvious — expect some scrambling and sidehilling on scree and rock benches. Total approach is roughly 6-7 miles and ~3,600-3,800 ft of gain one-way from the trailhead to the base of the summit block, consistent with the ~13-14 mile, ~4,800-5,600 ft round-trip character of this route.
approach_variant_names: Yellow Aster Butte Trail, then the Tomyhoi Arm ridge to the moat below the false summit
current.descent: Descend by reversing the Southeast Ridge line of ascent — there is no separate walk-off. From the true summit (7,439 ft), reverse the Class 3 summit block and the exposed ~40-ft gabled section of ridge back to the false summit, then downclimb the short wall to the notch at about 7,250 ft. This downclimb is the most exposed step on the route (big air on both sides), and many parties protect it rather than downclimbing free: previous climbing parties have left an informal rappel/lowering setup at the notch — a sling around a natural rock horn, not a bolted or fixed-chain anchor — good for one short (~15-20 ft) rappel or a doubled-rope lower/handline through the Class 3.5 slot. Inspect and back up any in-place tat before trusting it, or build your own natural anchor; a single 30m or longer rope doubled is plenty. Many parties skip the rappel entirely and instead downclimb this slot with a simple rope belay from above. Below the notch, reverse the traverse across the small snow/ice moat (can be firm or icy in morning conditions — an ice axe is worth carrying), continue back along the glacier's top edge and the north-side benches around the pinnacles, drop to the 6,266-ft col, climb back over the hump, and descend into the Yellow Aster Basin to rejoin the maintained trail. From there it's a straightforward but long descent back down the Yellow Aster Butte Trail to the trailhead; parties moving at a moderate pace should expect the descent to take nearly as long as the ascent (trip reports cite ~5 hours down), and finishing the lower trail by headlamp is common if the party is not fast.
current.detailed_rack: No technical gear required; a short rope can protect the summit block for less confident scramblers.
current.pro_needs: None to minimal.
bivy: Yellow Aster Butte tarns (Yellow Aster Meadows)
Twin Lakes Road upper section and the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead pullouts

name: Tooth and Claw
beta: Seven-pitch, 800-ft Grade IV 5.12a on the east side of the tower. The route alternates bolt-protected technical slab pitches (P1, P2, P5) with crack pitches (P3, P4, P6-P7) that need a full trad rack. Rock quality is noted as inconsistent, with looser sections on P1 and the P4 roof traverse. Descent is either a rappel of the route with two 70m ropes, or an exposed 4th-class traverse west from the East Shoulder to the same gully used by East Face parties.
overview: Tooth and Claw climbs the steep, sustained slabs directly right of the East Face, giving Lexington Tower's hardest free line at 5.12a. It is more pure slab/edge climbing and considerably less traveled than the neighboring wide-crack testpieces, first climbed by Steve Risse and Dave Tower in 1989.

current.approach: Same start as the East Face: from SR-20, park at the informal pullout on the north shoulder of the highway a short walk east of the small pond, about 1.2 miles east of Washington Pass (no permit needed). A well-beaten climbers' trail leaves the east end of the pond and climbs steeply through timber; in roughly 30 minutes it breaks out at the edge of the large boulder/talus field that lines the eastern base of the Liberty Bell group (Liberty Bell, Minuteman, Concord and Lexington Towers). From there, work up and left across the talus toward Lexington Tower's east side — 30-45 minutes total from the car to the base for most parties. There is no reliable water source along this approach (the roadside pond is not a water source worth using); carry what you need from the car. Snow can linger in the talus and at the base of the wall into early-mid summer and affects whether you gain the treed ledge from the left or right side. To reach the ledge itself, either climb a roped 5.8 pitch around a protruding block, or scramble one of the gullies flanking the ledge — both gullies see fairly frequent rockfall, so helmet up well before committing to them. Tooth and Claw begins near the left side of the treed ledge and angles rightward across slabs to the first bolt.
approach_variant_names: The hairpin pond pullout to the treed ledge, then its left side and rightward across slabs to the first bolt
current.descent: Two real options, and most parties take the walk-off. Option 1 (walk-off): from the East Shoulder, make an exposed, somewhat sketchy 4th-class traverse west (it borders on unprotected 5th-class slab in spots, so many parties stay roped) to gain the same descent gully used off the East Face. Downclimb the gully, then traverse north (right) to pick up the climbers'/cattle trail that runs up to Liberty Bell, which drops you onto the Blue Lake Trail; a faint climbers' path cuts off a final stretch of trail before the highway. Option 2 (rappel the route): from the top, the first anchor is a bolted station roughly 20-30 feet above the old P6 slung-block anchor. With double 70m ropes (a 70m lead line plus a 70m tag line) you can rappel from the very top of the route; doubled 60m ropes will not reach that first station. If you're bailing from above the P5 crux rather than finishing the route, two 60m ropes are workable using a fixed nut-and-sling anchor partway down P6 as an intermediate station — anything shorter risks coming up short between anchors. Lower down, the rappel stations are obvious, good-quality anchors on trees or bolts. Hardware is mixed vintage: some original 1989 5/16" bolts remain despite a post-2016 rebolting push, and at least one older fixed-nut/sling anchor is noted as aging — back up or inspect any anchor you didn't place yourself before weighting it.
current.detailed_rack: Doubles to 0.75 Camalot plus single #1, #2, and #3 Camalots cover the crack pitches (P3, P4, P6-P7); bring a full set of quickdraws for the well-bolted technical slab pitches (copperhead + 6 bolts on P1, bolted slab on P2 and the P5 crux). Two 70m ropes are ideal for the rappel descent; two 60m ropes work if stopping the rappels above P5.
rack: Cams, doubles to 0.75" Camalot plus single #1, #2, #3 Camalots
Full set of quickdraws for the bolted slab pitches (P1, P2, P5)
Two 70m ropes (lead + tag) for the route and rappel descent
current.pro_needs: Well-bolted on the technical slab pitches, but the crack pitches need a full complement of cams; loose rock on P1 and the P4 roof calls for careful placement and rope management to avoid dislodging blocks.
current.rope_note: 70m lead rope + 70m tagline ideal, allows rappelling from the very top.

name: Tooth - Chair Traverse
beta: Start up any of the standard routes on The Tooth (most parties use the South Face) to reach its summit, then follow the crest toward Chair Peak. The traverse mixes exposed 4th/low-5th-class scrambling and climbing on generally sub-par rock, with a short section of forest walking after leaving The Tooth, and one mandatory ~50-ft rappel off Bryant Peak partway along.
overview: A long ridge-crest linkup that continues past The Tooth's summit along the connecting ridge — over or past Bryant Peak — to finish atop Chair Peak, staying on or near the crest for nearly its full length.

current.approach: Begin via any Tooth route (historically the South Face) from the Alpental/Source Lake approach (~3,100 ft trailhead), then follow the crest toward Chair Peak: a short forested walking section right after the Tooth, exposed 4th/low-5th-class ridge travel, and a mandatory rappel off Bryant.
current.descent: Chair Peak's standard descent downclimbs from the summit to a saddle and continues down the steep, SW-facing gully back to the basin below; conditions and cornicing at the gully's head can vary through the season, so rope up or downclimb as conditions dictate.
current.detailed_rack: A small/light rock rack with an abundance of slings for extending over the exposed, wandering ridge crest; one 50m rope is reported as sufficient given the terrain and the single rappel.
current.pro_needs: Light protection is used mainly for the mandatory rappel and any short technical sections; much of the terrain is traveled unroped or simul-climbed by parties comfortable with 4th/low-5th-class exposure.

name: Top Gun
beta: Lead Sidewinder, then lower from its chains to the lip of the roof; from there, toprope back up through steep, technical moves to the shared anchor. Only about 30 ft, but sustained and powerful for the grade.
overview: A short, steep toprope problem exiting a roof below Pinto Rock's Sidewinder anchor, typically climbed as a second lap after leading Sidewinder.

current.approach: From Randle, WA on US Hwy 12: head south on SR 131, then follow NF-25 for 19.2 miles; just past milepost 21, turn left at the Mosquito Meadows sign onto NF-28 for 2.7 miles; turn left onto NF-77 (rough gravel, drive slowly) for about 2 miles until Pinto Rock comes into view at a large pullout. An evident use trail leads north from the pullout to the base of the formation (~0.3 mi/0.47 km). Top Gun is set up from the same location as Sidewinder on the North Side wall.
current.descent: Since Top Gun is rigged as a toprope off Sidewinder's existing bolted anchor, simply lower from the chains back to the base once finished; no separate rappel is needed.
current.detailed_rack: No rack needed beyond a toprope setup — built from Sidewinder's bolted anchor after leading and lowering.
current.pro_needs: None — climbed as a toprope off an existing sport anchor (Sidewinder's chains).
current.rope_note: Single-pitch sport route toproped/lowered off the same chain anchor as Sidewinder, over a roof lip; bolt-protected.

name: Tower Arete
beta: A more moderate alpine alternative to the North Tower Ridge Route, following an exciting arete with great exposure but lower technical difficulty. Route can be split into two parts: approach on easier terrain, then a more dramatic arete section. Requires careful attention to loose rock and boulders throughout. Approximately 4-5 hour total time from campground.
overview: A five-pitch alpine ridge route on the north face that follows the same ridge as the North Tower Ridge Route while avoiding its steeper, more technical pitches. Features excellent granite arete climbing with great exposure and views.

current.approach: Drive to Tiffany Springs Campground (elev. ~6,760 ft) via Forest Road 39, accessed either from Conconully (south, via FR-37) or from Winthrop (southwest, via East Chewuch Road and FR-37) — both are long gravel-road drives of an hour or more. From the campground, hike the Tiffany Lake Trail #373 east past Tiffany Lake to Honeymoon Pass (7,150 ft, roughly 45 minutes of easy trail), then leave the trail and traverse south across open grassy slopes to the small cirque at the base of the North Face (about 7,360 ft). The North Face itself rises roughly 650 feet above the cirque, split by couloirs and a rock tower; the whole approach is considered short and easy relative to other Pasayten-area objectives.
approach_variant_names: Tiffany Springs Campground and trail #373 over Honeymoon Pass, then the east slope traverse
current.descent: From the top of the Tower Arete, descend the northwest ridge (mostly 3rd class) to approximately 7,950 feet. Contour northeast and locate the old northeast ridge trail (may be faint). Follow it down to rejoin the main Tiffany Lake trail at Honeymoon Pass. Total descent time 1.5-2 hours.
current.detailed_rack: 60-meter rope essential for belays on steeper sections and rappel anchors if needed. Multiple extra-long slings for arete-top anchors and natural features. Light rack of cams and nuts (optional but recommended for self-rescue options).
current.pro_needs: Route can be managed with 60m rope and slings for natural-feature belays. Limited artificial protection available due to arete terrain; strong ropework skills and comfort on exposed terrain essential.
bivy: Tiffany Lake and Little Tiffany Lake
The talus and benches below the north face
current.rope_note: 4th-class arete/ridge scramble; a 60 m rope may be carried for exposed sections, but many parties solo it unroped.

name: North Couloir
beta: Climbed in the 1970s by John Roper, Don Avreitt, and Stu Ferguson; first skied in 2012 by Rowan Stewart and Alex Spoonde. Reached via Cascade Pass (or the nearby 'Alliteration Col') and a descent to Trapper Lake, the couloir is booted or skinned/booted from the lake basin, with ascent plates or crampons typically needed on firm crust higher up. Documented ascents run from January (icy) through late June (near-solstice corn/graupel), most commonly climbed/skied April-May.
overview: A prominent north-facing snow/ice couloir splitting Trapper Mountain's summit block above Trapper Lake, climbed on foot and skied/split-boarded as a steep ski-mountaineering descent.

current.approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (end of Cascade River Road, ~23.1 mi from Marblemount), travel via Cascade Pass or the nearby Alliteration Col and descend/traverse east through the Pelton Basin area to Trapper Lake (el. ~4,170 ft), sitting just northeast of Trapper Mountain. From the lake, boot or skin directly to the base of the obvious north-facing couloir splitting the summit block, switching to crampons/ski (ascent) plates as the snow firms up higher on the route.
approach_variant_names: Over the pass at the head of the river road, then east and down to the lake
From the valley on the east, reaching the lake basin from below
current.descent: The couloir is typically descended on skis/splitboard by the same line, managing sluff in the sustained 45-50 degree middle section; parties have encountered moats and debris (rock, fallen trees, ice chunks) piled at the base near Trapper Lake by early summer. From Trapper Lake, re-climb to Cascade Pass (or Alliteration Col) and follow the Cascade Pass Trail back to the trailhead; one documented car-to-car round trip took about 11.75 hours.
current.detailed_rack: No fixed rock protection is typically placed; a rope and pickets are optional depending on conditions.
current.pro_needs: Primarily a snow/ice couloir climb - protection is via ice axe/crampon technique rather than a placed rack; carry a rope and a few pickets if icy or firm conditions warrant belays.

name: East Slopes Scramble
beta: From the Stevens Pass Ski Area, climb the service road/trail past Skyline Lake to a gap in Skyline Ridge, then descend the ridge's north/back side into a creek drainage before climbing back up to gain Tye Peak's south ridge, which leads to the summit. There is no maintained trail; the route is class 2 terrain but requires route-finding and, outside of firm snow cover, pushing through dense brush. Tye Peak and neighboring Sky Mountain share the same approach and are often combined in one trip.
overview: Tye Peak (Pt. 5,476') is an unofficial name — it doesn't appear on USGS quads — for the summit rising directly above Stevens Pass on Skyline/Tye Ridge, between the Stevens Pass Ski Area and the Pacific Crest Trail corridor. The name comes from nearby Tye Lake and the Tye River. There's no maintained trail, and it draws little traffic, but its short approach from the highway makes it one of the fastest true summits in the corridor once the snow and brush clear.

current.approach: Park in the large day-use lot on the north side of US 2 right at the Stevens Pass summit (signed for the PCT/Skyline Lake trailhead); a Northwest Forest Pass or Forest Service day-use fee applies here. Leave from the lot beside the ski area's substation on the gated service road, and take the cairned left fork about a mile up to Skyline Lake and the gap in Skyline Ridge beyond it.
approach_variant_names: Skyline Lake and the ridge gap drop-in
current.descent: Most parties descend the same east-slope line, watching footing carefully on loose talus and scree in the upper section. Some instead drop off the south ridge or the southeast-facing slopes back toward Skyline Ridge — scout the line before committing, since both options funnel into brush lower down. Lingering snow patches on shaded aspects can still be glissaded or plunge-stepped into early July.
current.pro_needs: Non-technical class 2 scramble/snow climb — no rock rack is used.
current.rope_note: No trail to the summit; moderate-to-difficult summer bushwhack, commonly done instead as a winter snowshoe/scramble when brush is covered. Class 2 rating implies non-technical terrain.

name: Ultramega OK
beta: From Burgundy Col, descend around the north face to a twin-crack system with obvious loose blocks about 60 ft up (Action Potential's start is roughly 15 ft to the left). Eight pitches climb twin cracks, a chimney/right-facing corner, delicate face moves, and a bulging, thin-corner roof-traverse crux (P4, 5.11a) before wide cracks and chimneys and a final hand-crack/offwidth pitch reach the summit. Described by climbers as a good route that would be excellent with more traffic; some sections (notably the P6 corner) were noted as lichen-covered/dirty as of a 2018 ascent.
overview: Ultramega OK climbs the Northeast Buttress of Burgundy Spire — the hardest and least-traveled of the peak's four documented lines (5.11a, Grade III, 8 pitches, ~900 ft). From Burgundy Col, downclimb/scramble loose rock or steep snow around the north side of the spire to a twin-crack system marked by some obvious loose blocks about 60 ft up. The crux comes on P4, a thin corner leading into a roof at 5.11a; upper pitches traverse chimneys and cracks, with P8 finishing up an offwidth crack to the summit.

current.approach: Start at the long highway pullout on SR-20 (~4,310 ft, near milepost 166, roughly 3.75 mi east of Washington Pass and directly across the valley from Silver Star Mountain). A boot path drops east through loose talus into forest; look for a registration box a few minutes in. The path fords Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft (a swift wade in early season — trekking poles help). From the creek the trail climbs steadily east through forest and open slopes for roughly 2,200 ft to a broad flat bench/campsite around 6,460 ft, the approach's natural midpoint and a good high camp or bail point. Above the bench the boot path traverses loose scree gullies below Burgundy's northwest side and finishes up a final stretch of unstable, cairn-marked 'ball-bearing' scree over slab to Burgundy Col (~7,770–7,800 ft), the notch between Burgundy Spire and Paisano Pinnacle — about 3 miles and 3,500 ft one-way. From the col, Ultramega OK does not start at the col itself: scramble loose rock (or kick steps in lingering snow, ice axe recommended into July) down and around the base of Burgundy's north face until you reach a twin-crack system marked by obvious loose blocks about 60 ft up — this is the route start, climber's left of the North Face start, with Action Potential's clean splitter flake roughly 15 ft further left. Water is available at Early Winters Creek, a small trickle partway up near the col, and occasionally late-season ice on the col's east side. The loose final scree slopes below the col are the approach's main hazard — move carefully and stay bunched to avoid rockfall onto party members below.
approach_variant_names: The Wine Spires pullout and Burgundy Col, then further around the north face to the twin cracks with loose blocks
current.descent: Ultramega OK has no independent, well-established rappel line of its own — it is a Northeast Buttress route whose last pitch finishes up an offwidth crack to the summit, though a party that loses the line high up can traverse ledges into upper North Face terrain (near Burgundy Ledge) and finish from there. From wherever the route is topped out, the standard way down is the North Face's 5-rappel descent: ~40m from a heavily slung summit boulder down the middle of the upper face to a bolted ledge anchor; ~55m from the bolts down lichen-covered rock to a huge ledge near a rock arch (traverse the ledge to a constriction with slings); ~55m from that constriction down to a blue-slung horn; ~40m from the horn to broad scree ledges (watch the rope pull here — lots of snag potential); and a final ~60m back to Burgundy Col. Double 60m ropes make this clean; parties with a single 70m have reported getting down with some downclimbing between stances, but it's tighter on this line than on the standard North Face. From the base of the raps, reverse the Burgundy Col approach back to the highway. A few parties describe instead downclimbing loose 3rd/4th-class terrain on Burgundy's east side back toward the col to avoid rappelling altogether, but this is opportunistic route-finding rather than an established descent, and is not recommended in the wet or for parties unfamiliar with the terrain.
current.detailed_rack: Doubles of cams to #2, single #3 and #4 cams, and a nut set.
current.pro_needs: Sparse in spots, notably thin gear on the P4 corner-to-roof crux; a fuller rack (doubles to #2, singles #3/#4) covers the rest.
bivy: Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side

name: Southeast Slopes Scramble
beta: From the Smithbrook Road trailhead, hike the Smithbrook Trail roughly 0.9 mile up through old-growth forest to its junction with the Pacific Crest Trail near Union Gap. Leave the trail after a short distance and bushwhack northeast to gain Union Peak's southeast ridge at about 5,200 ft, then follow the ridge to the 5,696-5,700 ft summit. The line is an easy-to-moderate, non-technical alpine scramble in summer/fall and a moderate winter scramble or backcountry ski/snowshoe objective the rest of the year.
overview: Union Peak is a minor but scenic summit on the ridge crest just northeast of Stevens Pass, reached by a short approach up the Smithbrook Trail to Union Gap on the Pacific Crest Trail before a bushwhack/use-trail ascent of the peak's southeast ridge. It sits between Lichtenberg Mountain (to the southwest, above Lake Valhalla) and Jove Peak (6,007 ft, to the northeast); the two are commonly combined into one scramble day via the connecting saddle. In winter the same slopes become a popular backcountry ski and snowshoe objective, though avalanche hazard on all aspects makes it a far more serious undertaking than the summer scramble.

current.approach: Drive US 2 to Smithbrook Road (Forest Road 6700); the turnoff is about 4.2 miles east of Stevens Pass summit (roughly half a mile east of milepost 69 coming from the Leavenworth/Wenatchee side, or about 68 miles from Everett/Seattle). Follow FR 6700 about 2.7-3 miles to the Smithbrook Trailhead (~4,000 ft) on the left; the gravel road is normally passable to passenger cars once it's snow-free but is not plowed in winter, when parking shifts to a highway-side pullout and adds miles of road travel each way. From the trailhead, Smithbrook Trail #1590 climbs about 1 mile to the PCT junction at Union Gap, where the scramble begins.
approach_variant_names: Smithbrook Trail to Union Gap
current.descent: Descend the same southeast ridge and use-trail back to the PCT junction at Union Gap, then follow the PCT and Smithbrook Trail back to the trailhead. No rappels or technical downclimbing are required; the main task is not losing the faint, unmarked boot path back into the trees. Parties who continued on to Jove Peak typically return the same way over Union rather than descending Jove's other faces, which are steeper and more avalanche-exposed in season.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed — this is an unroped Class 2 scramble on maintained trail, a short bushwhack, and an open ridge/meadow to the summit.
current.pro_needs: No technical protection required for the standard route; footwear with good traction and trekking poles are the main 'gear' concern for the steep, loose rib section.
current.rope_note: From Smithbrook Rd/Union Gap, bushwhack NE to gain the SE ridge and follow it to the summit. It is an easy to moderate, non-technical alpine scramble.

name: Unknown Climb Up the Castle
beta: The Castle is a spire north of the main Dikes climbing area, with two bolted climbs to its top. Rock quality is poor and the approach is a bushwhack/scramble, but the exposure and summit view are notable.
overview: Route on The Castle, a small 45-foot pinnacle on a ridge west of Spangler Creek confluence.

current.approach: The Dikes sit in the Umatilla National Forest's Walla Walla Ranger District, in the East Fork Touchet River valley near Ski Bluewood, southeast Washington — not near the Snake River. Access is via North Touchet Road out of Dayton, WA, paved for roughly the first 15-16 miles before becoming gravel Forest Service Road 64 at the forest boundary; the road continues to Ski Bluewood and stays in use through winter, but snow on the crags and approach slopes keeps the climbing season to roughly May-October, sometimes from April. Approaches are very short and roadside: the south Megadike is reached by parking near a bridge 1.2 miles past the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead and scrambling directly up the steep hillside above the bridge abutment, while Weeping Wall and Joe's Rock are similar short pullout-to-cliff scrambles at 1.1 and 2.0 miles past the same trailhead respectively. The area is lightly visited and faint-trailed, and the basalt is notably loose/fractured, requiring routine loose-rock cleaning. This route is on The Castle: from the Middle Point Ridge Trailhead, continue about 1.2 miles further down the road (0.6 miles past where The Castle first becomes visible on the ridge) and park on the right (east) side where a dirt road from the Spangler Creek valley intersects the main road. Climb a long, very steep hillside to the base of the pinnacle.
current.descent: Single short pitch (~40 ft) to the ~45 ft spire's summit; lower or rappel from the bolted anchor on a single strand.
current.detailed_rack: Fully bolted line up the spire; standard short-route sport rack.
current.pro_needs: Fully bolted, but rock quality is explicitly noted as poor — test holds carefully.
current.rope_note: Single-pitch bolted sport route at The Castle sub-area of The Dikes, WA (approached via a long, steep hillside to the pinnacle base). The pitch is about 40 ft; 70m recommended given crag-wide walls up to 140ft.

name: Unnamed  2
beta: Bolted sport route in the Alpenkuhl area. Quality granite with good rock and solid protection.
overview: Sport climbing route on south-facing granite wall

current.approach: Spire Gully right (Alpenkuhl), part of the Hairpin Crags, is reached from the same large pullout at the hairpin turns on SR-20 near Washington Pass used for Kangaroo Temple. Looking up toward South Early Winter Spire from the pullout, Spire Gully is the obvious gully just below and left; Alpenkuhl is its sunnier, south-facing right side (the left side is known as Tiger Wall). The approach is one of the shortest at Washington Pass — a direct walk/scramble of roughly 10-15 minutes straight up from the highway, snow-covered in early season and a worn boot path later in summer.
current.descent: Tops out at a fixed bolted anchor at the top of the headwall. Lower directly to the ground on a single rope; no walk-off or rappel is required given the short, single-pitch length.
current.rope_note: Spire Gully right - Alpenkuhl (Washington Pass bolted crag, 7min walk from hairpin). Recorded as 5.9, sport, single pitch.

current.detailed_rack: Several fixed bolts protect the lower wall; above the last bolt, roughly 30 feet of crux climbing through the roof has no fixed protection and requires trad gear up to about 2 inches.
current.pro_needs: Quickdraws for the bolted section plus a small trad rack (to about 2 inches) for the unbolted crux roof.
current.rope_note: Spire Gully right - Alpenkuhl. Recorded as 5.8+, trad (only trad route in this otherwise-bolted cluster) - needs a real rack, not just draws.

Looking up toward South Early Winter Spire from the pullout, Spire Gully is the obvious gully just below and left; Alpenkuhl is its sunnier, south-facing right side (the left side is known as Tiger Wall).
