current.pro_needs: Fully bolted, 7 bolts to the anchor.
current.rope_note: Spire Gully right - Alpenkuhl. Recorded as 5.8, sport, single pitch.

name: Up In Arms
beta: Six sustained pitches of corners and cracks, climbed all free, up a sunny, southwest-facing wall; the hardest climbing is on pitch one. Three fixed protection bolts and one bolted anchor supplement gear. The route earned a 3-star rating in its first documented ascents.
overview: A modern (2023) six-pitch 5.11 testpiece up the southwest face of Concord Tower, well left of the older south-face routes and the closest of the tower's lines to the Blue Lake Trailhead.

current.approach: Follow the Blue Lake Trail toward the Beckey Gully; just as you reach Concord Tower's west face, head uphill staying close to the wall to the base of the route, well to climber's left of the South Face routes.
current.descent: From the summit, make two rappels using a single 60 m rope down to the Concord/Lexington notch, then walk off down the shared gully back toward the Blue Lake Trail — approach shoes are worth carrying for this.
current.detailed_rack: Doubles from about 0.2 to 3 inches plus a single 4-inch cam, and plenty of slings/alpine draws; three fixed protection bolts and one bolted anchor supplement the gear on lead. A 60 m rope is used for both leading and the rappel descent.
current.pro_needs: A doubled cam rack (0.2-3in) plus a #4, supplemented by 3 bolts and 1 bolted anchor.

name: Upper North Ridge w/Great Gendarme
beta: Grade IV, 5.9. Eleven pitches of low/mid 5th class (5.5-5.6) to Great Gendarme; two crux pitches of 5.9 on the Gendarme itself (steep hand/finger dihedral and offwidth requiring 3.5 protection). Hazards: knife-edge ridge with 1,000+ feet of exposure, loose rock, variable snow/ice conditions, wet terrain mid-ridge, cold wind on exposed ridge, rockfall from climber traffic, steep descent terrain. Requires advanced alpine rock climbing skills, crack protection (especially 3.5"), excellent weather judgment, overnight bivy capability. Total climbing time: 16-20 hours car-to-car. Best months: June-August (snow dependent).
overview: Climbs the upper ~1,200 feet of Mount Stuart's famous North Ridge from the notch below the Great Gendarme, following exposed 4th-to-mid-5th-class ridge crest to two steep 5.9 pitches on the Gendarme itself, then easier terrain to the summit.

current.approach: From I-90 Exit 85, take Highway 970 east 7 miles to Teanaway Road, then bear right onto North Fork Teanaway Road continuing 22.5 miles total. From trailhead: via Lake Ingalls and Stuart Pass to Goat Pass, then east across the Stuart Glacier to the North Ridge notch
approach_variant_names: Goat Pass and the Stuart Glacier to the fourth-class gully and the notch
Mountaineer Creek and the Stuart Glacier from the north
current.descent: From the true summit, travel southeast on blocky 3rd/4th-class terrain toward the false summit, follow cairns down into the Cascadian Couloir snowfield, then descend extended 3rd-class scree/talus to Ingalls Creek. Sherpa Glacier or a Sherpa Pass glissade are faster early-season alternatives for parties returning to a north-side camp.
current.detailed_rack: Standard alpine trad rack: nuts, cams to roughly 3.5in (a single wide piece for the Gendarme offwidth), doubles in common finger-to-hand sizes, and long slings for wandering ridge belays.
rack: Cams, doubles 0.5-3" (finger-to-hand sizes) plus one 4" piece for the offwidth
Long slings for wandering ridge belays
current.pro_needs: Protection on the ridge pitches is described by climbers as 'pretty subjective' — natural gear supplements a standard rack; the Gendarme offwidth wants a dedicated wide piece.
bivy: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
current.rope_note: One of the Fifty Classic Climbs. ~11 pitches of low/mid 5th from the Stuart Glacier notch to the Gendarme base, then two crux 5.9 pitches plus a 5.8-5.9 pitch before 3 final low-5th pitches. A fixed #4 Camalot has been reported in place on the offwidth.

name: Vanishing Point
beta: Vanishing Point is approximately as steep a route as one could find on the mountain—sustained, largely overhanging climbing, with most pitches at 5.11–5.12 and several at 5.10. The route was established over several years and fully modernized in 2020 with new stainless-steel anchors and improved protection. Notable features include the crux 5.12 pitch out a huge roof (pitch 11), a collapsed roof section, and several intentionally runout pitches. The approach involves 800 feet of mostly roped-up slab climbing with fixed lines and bolts. Published pitch counts vary between 14 and 20 depending on how the climbing is split or linked; the pitch-by-pitch breakdown here uses the 14-pitch convention.
overview: A nearly 1,500-foot overhanging prow of very sustained alpine climbing at 5.11+/5.12, featuring multiple roof systems, technical arete climbing, and serious exposure throughout. One of the most demanding alpine climbs in the Cascades.

current.approach: Start at Barclay Lake trailhead (74920 NE Stevens Pass Hwy, Skykomish, WA 98288). Follow the pleasant level main trail for about 20 minutes to a bridge crossing a large creek (~1 mile). Before the bridge, break right into forest around a large boulder, then walk through relatively open forest or along the creek bed until reaching an open boulder field. Continue through the boulder field to reach steep gullies. Climb around the right side of a chossy waterfall (exposed scrambling). Continue up the wash to a ramp with hand lines, then up a 60–70° forested rib with fixed lines and natural protection, then approximately 800 feet of mostly roped-up slab via bolted sections and natural features. Total approach time: 2.5–3.5 hours for competent parties.
approach_variant_names: Barclay Creek Trail, right before the bridge, fixed lines to the tower
current.descent: From the summit, descend via the established base jumper trail system (marked on climbing area maps). The descent is non-technical but lengthy. Follow the forested ridge and switchback trail through old-growth forest back down to the Barclay Lake trailhead. The descent can be muddy and root-strewn; allow 3 hours total for descent and return to parking.
current.detailed_rack: Single rack to #1 with a few duplicates in the finger sizes. Recommended: 2–3 nuts in fingers, 2–3 mid-hand nuts, 2–3 hand-sized cams, 1–2 #1 cams. Small to medium nuts and slings optional but not required. 15 draws (mix of singles and doubles) recommended; 6 of these can be single runners.
current.pro_needs: Primarily bolted sport climbing with some trad pitches. Anchors are bolted throughout; the bolts were replaced with stainless steel and upgraded during 2020 modernization. Climbers must be comfortable with self-rescue, anchor building, and transitioning between bolted and trad protection. The route involves high commitment and serious altitude—turnaround decisions should be made early.

name: Standard Route (Ares Tower)
beta: This is the standard line up the ridge's true high point, first climbed by Fred Beckey and Herb Staley in 1952. From Burgundy Col, work north along/just below the ridge crest on 4th-class rock to a notch on the north side of the summit block, then scramble south around the west side of a large summit boulder to the base of a short low-5th-class step that gains the true summit. An old fixed rappel anchor sits at the top for the descent. Most parties do it as a long day from the Washington Pass pullout, and many combine it with the neighboring Acropolis and Niki Tower to the south for an efficient multi-summit day on the ridge.
overview: Ares Tower is the highest of several named granite spires — Charon Tower, The Acropolis, Ares Tower, Vasiliki Tower, the Juno-Jupiter Towers, Aphrodite Tower, and Baccus Tower — strung along Vasiliki Ridge, which radiates north from the Wine Spires/Silver Star Mountain massif above Washington Pass. Fred Beckey and Herb Staley made the first ascent of the ridge on May 31, 1952; Beckey named it after Vasiliki Dwyer, a woman he met at Stevens Pass — the only Cascades feature he ever named after a woman. Despite its imposing look from the highway, Ares Tower itself is a moderate objective: essentially a 4th-class scramble to a notch just north of the true summit, finished by a short low-5th-class step (or an alternate direct low-5th variation up the west face).

current.approach: Park at the unsigned 'Wine Spires' pullout on SR-20, about 3.7 miles east of Washington Pass (roughly 0.7 mile past the Cutthroat Lake Road turnoff, near milepost 166), at about 4,300 ft elevation. A boot path drops down loose, scree-covered talus into the trees, passes a trail register, and crosses Early Winters Creek on logs at about 4,080 ft. The trail then climbs steadily through forest, steepening between two side creeks, gaining roughly 3,700+ ft to Burgundy Col (~7,800 ft); a flat bench campsite ('the Bench,' ~6,460 ft) sits about halfway up and is the more common camp for this objective. Vasiliki Ridge and Ares Tower rise directly north of Burgundy Col and the Wine Spires camp area; from the bench or col, contour and scramble north along the ridge crest to reach the base of Ares Tower.
approach_variant_names: The Wine Spires pullout to the Bench, then north along the ridge crest to Ares Tower
current.descent: Rappel from the fixed anchor at the Ares Tower summit down to the notch to retrieve stashed gear, then reverse the 4th-class ridge scramble and descend the Burgundy Col approach trail back to Early Winters Creek and the SR-20 pullout.
current.detailed_rack: Standard alpine rock rack (cams and nuts) with slings for the spire pitches
current.pro_needs: Rock protection on the technical pitches; belayed climbing
bivy: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout

name: Voile Normale
beta: Ascend along the SW spur, heading east to a broken ledge with a tree on the left. Climb up and left over a short slab to a notch, then through the notch and along a terraced ledge to a gully on the crest of the SW spur. Continue along the scree terrace below the summit block, then descend to the prominent tree visible from the road and climb the long crack to the summit.
overview: The 'standard/normal route' up Steeple Rock's SW spur, and the shared finish for the East Ridge line.

current.approach: Park in the pullout on Obstruction Point Road below Steeple Rock; start directly on the SW spur, no trail.
current.descent: (no DESCENT section on this route's page)

name: Southeast Peak Standard (Home Lake approach)
beta: This is the primary route to Warrior Peak's Southeast Summit. The route involves approximately 9-10 miles of approach hiking, making it a typical 2-day backpacking objective. From the cirque below the peak, ascend the obvious couloir between the SE and NW summits. If snow-filled (common early season), the couloir is steep and straightforward; if melted out, it's loose scree. Above the couloir, scramble to a saddle at approximately 7,000 feet, then climb steep snow or a snow moat to reach the exposed rock section. Some parties rope this short pitch; others solo it depending on conditions and skill.
overview: A striking twin-summit massif in the eastern Olympics, rising immediately north of Mount Constance (its nearest higher neighbor, 0.8 mi south-southeast) within the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park. Warrior is the 11th-highest peak in the Olympic Range, built of Eocene-era pillow basalt uplifted with the range's obducted oceanic crust. Fred Beckey made the first ascent solo in 1945, climbing both the northwest and southeast (true, higher) summits in one push and naming the mountain; he's said to have carved his name into a rock at the saddle between the two summits, which some later parties report still finding.

current.approach: Drive Highway 101 to Sequim Bay State Park area, turn left on Louella Road for 1 mile, then left on Palo Alto Road for about 5.8 miles (it becomes FS Road 28 at the Forest Boundary), then turn right onto FS Road 2880, drive past Dungeness Forks Campground for 1 mile, stay left onto FS Road 2870 for 8.7 miles to Upper Dungeness Trailhead. Upper Dungeness Trail is the shortest and easiest approach. Hike the trail 3.4 miles and 600 feet to Camp Handy, then take the left fork and continue 3 miles and 1,850 feet to Boulder Camp (total: 6.4 miles, 2,450 feet gain). From Boulder Camp, continue south approximately 1.5-2 miles, crossing creeks, until you reach the final larger creek that flows from the cirque SE of Warrior Peak. Continue past this creek to a boulder field, then head up and back left toward the creek, staying under a band of cliffs, and continue up the boulders approximately 1 mile and 1,200 feet to reach the cirque at approximately 5,900 feet.
approach_variant_names: Upper Dungeness Trail, Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter to the southeast cirque
Home Lake basecamp, from either the Dungeness or the Dosewallips side
current.descent: Reverse the route: downclimb or carefully descend the crux rock step back to the ~7,000 ft saddle, then descend the couloir and cirque back toward Home Lake. Parties describe the snow chute descent as fast and consequential if glissaded without a clear view of the runout — at least one party described nearly going over a cliff band while glissading nearby terrain, and rockfall in the gully is a recurring hazard, so keep parties spread out and avoid glissading unless the full runout is visible and safe.
current.detailed_rack: A short rope and a light alpine rack (a few nuts and small cams, slings) are commonly carried to protect or belay the exposed summit-block moves.
current.pro_needs: Protection for short low-5th-class steps on the summit block; most of the route is Class 3-4 scrambling.
bivy: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park

name: Washington Ellinor Traverse (Ridge)
beta: From Washington's summit, follow the narrow crest of fractured pillow basalt southwest toward Ellinor. The initial 'Wedge' gives about 150 ft of positive, low-5th/class-4 climbing — the best section on the route. Beyond it the ridge continues as sustained class-4 scrambling past a series of gendarmes (hidden ledges usually keep difficulty at class 4 or below), with one loose ~50 ft downclimb considered the least enjoyable section. Where the ridge gets too difficult or exposed to continue unroped, most parties drop into the basin below and either downclimb a technical sequence or bypass it on a snow finger to rejoin Ellinor's standard winter route to that summit. An alternative some parties recommend over the direct ridge: the standard west-side basin traverse into Ellinor's NE couloir.
overview: A committing, mostly unroped ridge traverse linking Mount Washington and Mount Ellinor across a narrow crest of fractured, weathered pillow basalt. Most parties climb Mount Washington's standard scramble route first, then follow the connecting ridge across a series of gendarmes and an exposed low-5th-class 'Wedge' section before descending via Mount Ellinor's standard trail. The crux is a short, notably loose downclimb near the ridge's low point; sustained exposure and inconsistent rock quality make this a serious outing for confident scramblers/climbers only, not a beginner objective.

current.approach: Climb Mount Washington first via its standard south route from the FR 2419 trailhead (see the Standard Route). The traverse itself has no separate trailhead or approach — it begins directly from Washington's summit, heading southwest along the connecting ridge toward Mt. Ellinor rather than descending Washington's standard route.
approach_variant_names: Climb Mount Washington first from FR-2419 — the traverse starts on its summit
current.descent: Most parties continue the traverse to Mount Ellinor's summit and descend via Mount Ellinor's standard trail (upper trailhead off a spur of FR-2419, the same North Lake Cushman Road corridor used for the approach); parties can also reverse the traverse back over Mount Washington to its own trailhead.
current.detailed_rack: Most parties carry only a small rack or none at all, since gear placements in the poor basalt are marginal; a few slings for the gendarmes and a short rope for the loose downclimb are reasonable options for less confident parties.
rack: A few slings for gendarme anchors (natural pro on horns/chockstones)
Light supplemental rack: small nuts/cams where the fractured basalt allows
Short handline/rope for the loose crux downclimb (optional)
current.pro_needs: No fixed protection on route; a short handline or a few slings are sometimes used by parties to protect the loose crux gendarme downclimb, but the traverse is typically done unroped by experienced parties in dry conditions.
current.rope_note: Grade II alpine trad/snow route; published descriptions explicitly state that the rock is horrible and the protection problematic on the fractured basalt, so natural pro on horns/chockstones is often more reliable than cams/nuts. The ~150 ft low-5th 'Wedge' near the start is the best climbing; the crux is the loose gendarme downclimb near the ridge's low point.

name: Waterfall Buttress
beta: Ascends the rib left of Roan Wall's major slab waterfall, which gives the route some protection from snow/debris shed from above — though the base is still commonly buried under residual avalanche snow for much of the climbing season. Facing east, it gets direct morning sun and afternoon shade. Climbing is a varied mix of bolted face and mostly-thin cracks; described as a modern Darrington-area classic with some climbing more reminiscent of Index or Yosemite than typical Darrington granite.
overview: A 6-pitch, 800-foot Grade III alpine rock route up the prominent rib above the Martha's Place bivy boulder, mixing bolted face climbing with thin cracks on quality granite.

current.approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to the Arlington exit, then SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, and turn onto Squire Creek Road at the west end of town, following it to the parking area where it's gated off by washout damage. From there the approach is long and rough: hike the old roadbed past a landslide crossing (~5 minutes in), reach the original road end around 30-40 minutes from the car, then follow a faint trail through a dry streambed and alder brush, ford Squire Creek, and pick through obscure forest track before finally breaking out into the open basin roughly 2 hours from the car. This is a known bushwhacky, unmaintained approach typical of Darrington-area crags, with route-finding (flagging, cairns) required in several spots.
approach_variant_names: Squire Creek road walk, white-boulder streambed and ford into Waterfall Basin
current.descent: Descend by rappelling the route with double 60m ropes. On the lower-angle section, stay skier's-right to avoid dropping into the adjacent gully and creek below the slab waterfall.
current.detailed_rack: Medium rack of cams and nuts to 2 inches, with extra pieces smaller than 1 inch. All belays and rappel anchors are bolted.
current.pro_needs: Mostly bolt-protected face climbing supplemented by natural gear on the thin crack sections; a medium rack to 2" with extra small pieces covers it.
bivy: Squire Creek road end / trailhead bivouac
Squire Creek Park & Campground, Snohomish County

name: Standard Route (South Ridge / South Gully via Copper Glance Basin)
beta: Approach via the Copper Glance Trail to Copper Glance Lake and the upper basin below Isabella Ridge, camp or day-trip from there, then ascend talus/scree and a south-facing gully to the south ridge and follow it to the summit. Commonly combined with an ascent of neighboring Big Craggy Peak (connected by a ridge/saddle) in the same trip. Loose rock (choss) and lingering snow in the gully are the main technical considerations; route is class 2 with brief class 2-3 scrambling in places.
overview: The standard route climbs West Craggy's south side from a high camp in Copper Glance Basin: talus and scree lead to a gully/chute below the south ridge (often holding snow into summer), which tops out on an easy summit ridge walk. No roped climbing is required in summer conditions.

current.approach: From Winthrop, drive north about 8 miles on West Chewuch Road (County Road 1213) to Eightmile Road (Forest Road 5130), then continue roughly 12-15 miles northwest along Eightmile Creek to the Copper Glance Trailhead (about 3,800-3,810 ft; no fee). Hike Copper Glance Trail #519, which begins on an old mining-claim jeep track/tramway grade (FSR 505) for about 1.5 miles to the historic Copper Glance mine, crosses Copper Glance Creek (the creek's bridge has been reported washed out or missing in some years, requiring a ford), and continues through a 2018 burn area past a small pond to Copper Glance Lake and the open upper basin below Isabella Ridge (about 3.3-3.5 miles one-way, ~6,260-6,600 ft) — a common camp/base for the peak.
approach_variant_names: Copper Glance Basin and the south-side chute
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb the south ridge back into the gully/chute and descend the loose scree and talus to the upper basin. Where snow remains, an ice axe (and crampons/microspikes if firm) is useful, and glissading the snow sections can speed descent when conditions allow. Below the basin, retrace the Copper Glance Trail past the mine site and back down the old tramway grade to the trailhead, re-fording Copper Glance Creek where the bridge is out.
current.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard summer route.
current.pro_needs: None - the standard route is unroped scrambling; no fixed or removable protection is placed.

name: West Face
beta: A premier alpine testpiece featuring five pitches of high-quality granite climbing to the summit terrace, plus a short sixth pitch up an easy chimney to the summit. The route climbs splitter cracks and exposed face climbing over 600 vertical feet. Pitch 2 contains the crux with thin cracks, bulbous knobs, and a small roof. The climbing features varied terrain including incipient flakes, stemming, and lieback sections. Protection is generally reliable on white granite. The onsight first free ascent in 2007 was completed with no falls. Descent via four double-rope rappels from the summit.
overview: The West Face of North Peak is one of the Cascades' sheerest and cleanest granite faces, offering world-class alpine rock climbing. The route ascends the center of the face with excellent crack and face climbing on solid white granite. Originally established as an aid route in 1986, the first free ascent in 2007 demonstrated the exceptional quality of the line, with sustained 5.11 climbing featuring hard crack work, bulbous knobs, lieback sections, and wild exposure.

current.approach: The standard approach is from the Downey Creek Trailhead (off Suiattle River Road) via the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse — a rugged, largely off-trail alpine route over Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek involving glacier travel and significant bushwhacking. Climbers typically budget a full day (or two) of approach before reaching the base of North Peak's granite West Face; this is an experienced-mountaineers-only objective, not a roadside crag.
approach_variant_names: Downey Creek, Itswoot Ridge and the Dome-Chikamin col
current.descent: Rappel down the center of the West Face via four consecutive double-rope rappels of roughly 50 m, 50 m, 50 m and 20 m, using natural anchor features and existing bolt/gear anchors established on the granite. Ensure proper rope management to avoid tangling on the steep granite face. Once back at the base of the route, climb back up to the Chikamin-Dome Col via the Chickamin Glacier approach, watching carefully for crevasses and potential moat crossings. From the col, descend the cross-country route back to Bachelor Flats (taking approximately 8-10 hours depending on snow coverage and conditions). From Bachelor Flats, follow the Downey Creek trail back to the trailhead (6-8 hours depending on fitness and pack weight). Plan on getting back to the col the day you climb, then two days out to the car.
current.detailed_rack: For the West Face on North Peak, bring a complete rack of cams from #0.5 to #3 for the thin crack climbing on pitches 1-2 and the crux, supplemented with wires #1-#8 for protection on flakes and knobs. Small stoppers are useful for incipient crack sections. Quickdraws for both natural protection and any bolted anchors. The rock is solid white granite with reliable placements. Bring a 60m single dynamic rope and basic alpine rock climbing gear. Thin hands to finger cracks are essential for pitches with incipient placements.
rack: Cams, doubles 0.1-3" (triples in tips/finger sizes recommended)
current.pro_needs: This is a serious alpine rock route requiring expert-level crack climbing protection skills. Protection is generally available but requires solid understanding of gear placement in granite. The crux pitches (especially pitch 2) demand confident lead climbing and protection placement at 5.11 difficulty. Pitches with thin cracks and bulbous knobs require precision protection. The onsight nature of the first free ascent speaks to the quality of the granite and availability of natural protection.
bivy: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
current.rope_note: 6-pitch, 600ft alpine rock route; a 60m lead rope, plus a second 60m rope for the double-rope descent rappels. Upper section has newer bolted rap stations; original descent raps off a large chockstone.

name: West Ridge
beta: A hidden-gem moderate that has become cleaner and more popular over the years. The line rambles up cracks and the ridge crest with sustained mid-fifth-class climbing throughout; the crux comes about halfway up, on pitch 4, on a short section of steep twin finger cracks, and the final pitch is an exposed, runout 5.8 face regarded by many parties as the route's real ("mental") crux. Often camped for and combined with the North Face of Burgundy Spire for a ~12-13 pitch link-up day.
overview: The West Ridge climbs the crest of Paisano Pinnacle in 7-8 pitches of sustained, high-quality 5.8+ hand and finger cracks with big comfortable belay ledges, widely regarded as one of the best moderate alpine rock routes at Washington Pass.

current.approach: Follow the shared Wine Spires trail: boot path down talus to Early Winters Creek, cross on a log, then climb steeply up the timbered rib north of Burgundy Creek to the ~6,500 ft basin/camp (roughly 2 hours from the car). Paisano Pinnacle's West Ridge route starts lower than Burgundy Spire's and is commonly linked with Burgundy Spire's North Face in one long car-to-car day; fresh water is reported from a spring near the camp bench.
approach_variant_names: Unsigned highway pullout east of Washington Pass, the timbered rib to the bench, then the contour right
current.descent: From the summit, downclimb easier terrain for a few hundred feet, then make two rappels — 30m and 20m — down into the gully beneath Burgundy Col, downclimbing sections between the rappel anchors. From the gully, follow the climbers' trail back down past the bench camp, cross Early Winters Creek, and finish with a short climb back up to the highway pullout.
current.detailed_rack: A single set of nuts plus cams from roughly 0.4 in to 4 in; a single #4 cam is generally sufficient, but doubles in finger/hand sizes are recommended for the splitter crack pitches. A small cam (~0.2 in or equivalent) is important for the runout final pitch.
rack: Cams, 0.4-4" (small cams useful on twin cracks P3-4; a wide piece for the P8 crack)
current.pro_needs: Gear to 4 inches protects most of the route well; the final 5.8 pitch is the exception: above its widening crack, the face section has sparse protection, with a small cam the key piece.
bivy: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
current.rope_note: 8 pitches/600ft, Grade III; two rappels off pre-placed sling/horn anchors for descent.

name: South Route
beta: Approached from a multi-day camp in Crescent Creek Basin (reached via the Goodell Creek / Terror Creek / Barrier approach), the route crosses roughly a mile of basin terrain before climbing a chockstone-filled gully system rated up to 5.7 (also given as South Face, Grade II, 5th class). Loose rock and route-finding are the main challenges; parties commonly climb this as a side objective from a Southern Pickets base camp rather than a stand-alone trailhead-to-summit day.
overview: West Twin Needle (7,936 ft) is the taller, western spire of the Twin Needles, a pair of rock pinnacles in the Southern Pickets immediately west of Mount Terror. Its slightly lower twin to the east (about 7,840+ ft) is the more technically serious of the pair; West Twin Needle carries easier class 2-3 flanks but this South Route tackles steeper 5.7 rock directly up its south/east side above Crescent Creek Basin. First climbed August 17, 1932 by William Degenhardt, James Martin, and Herb Strandberg, it sees very few ascents each year owing to the multi-day cross-country approach required to reach it.

current.approach: Start at the Goodell Creek Cross-Country Zone trailhead off SR-20 just west of Newhalem (this is the drive-in endpoint). From the trailhead, follow the climbers' path up the old, overgrown Goodell Creek logging-road corridor through open forest for roughly 3.5 miles; beyond the fork where the maintained tread ends, the route becomes a boot path through talus with only sparse flagging, so follow cairns rather than a continuous trail. This talus/boulder-hopping stretch leads to a crossing of Terror Creek — look for a cairn marking the ford; water levels are seasonal and the crossing can go from a rock-hop in late season to a genuinely wet, current-fed ford in early summer or after rain. Beyond the creek, the route climbs a steep, brushy rib known informally as 'the Barrier': tree debris, slide alder, and a faded, easy-to-lose boot path make this the route-finding crux of the approach. Water becomes scarce above about 5400 ft — expect only dry streambeds and the occasional small puddle, so treat any water below the Barrier as your last reliable fill-up. The path tops out and drops about 200 ft into Crescent Creek Basin, then traverses roughly a mile north across scree to the common Southern Pickets camp below Mount Terror at about 6050 ft, fed by two streams coming off the slabs above (reliable water and the standard base camp for this side of the range). From camp, West Twin Needle's south side presents two gullies right of a dividing buttress; the true line follows a minor rib on climber's left of the rightmost gully (which cliffs out in a closed chimney) up to a notch at about 7400 ft below the Eye Col, the gap between the two Twin Needles. The technical crux of the approach is pitching through this 'Eye Col' gully past large chockstones on low 5th-class rock, including one narrow-crack pitch typically taken on a belay. From the notch, easy slabs and scrambling (roughly 5.7) lead to the summit. Total round trip from the trailhead runs about 19.5 miles (~31 km) with well over 7000 ft of gain. Expect loose rock throughout the gullies, sustained route-finding through brush and scree, exposed scrambling on the connecting ribs, and unreliable water above the Barrier.
approach_variant_names: Crescent Creek Basin camp to the Eye Col gully
current.descent: Rather than reversing the ascent gully to the Eye Col, descend the class 2–3 west face to the Himmelhorn–West Twin Needle notch on the far side of the peak. Below that, plan on 2 rappels using doubled 60m ropes to get past a band of vertical slabs — parties report the first anchor built on a protruding rock angled upward (to keep a rappel sling from walking off) and a second anchor set above boulders in the south gully; treat these as natural/gear anchors rather than fixed bolted stations; bring cord/rap rings since existing tat should not be counted on. From the base of the rappels, grassy benches sit around 6800 ft; from there traverse east and climb back up roughly 200 ft to regain the 'left gully,' which is then downclimbed/scrambled to the base near the buttress that splits the approach gullies. From there, retrace the south-route approach line back down through Crescent Creek Basin to camp. Where conditions and the exact line allow, some parties instead reverse the east-face gully (class 2–3) directly into Crescent Creek Basin, avoiding the technical col rappels entirely but at the cost of more sustained loose, exposed scrambling — this is the non-technical walk-off alternative referenced in older route notes. Watch for loose blocks throughout and be prepared for stuck ropes on retrieval (reported by at least one party, freed with a hard tug) — a real risk on this kind of low-angle-slab rappel line.
current.detailed_rack: A light alpine rock rack (small-to-mid cams and nuts) covers the low-5th-class pitches and 5.7 crux; carry a few extra slings/quickdraws for the chockstone-choked gully sections.
current.pro_needs: Standard rock rack to ~2-3 inches is sufficient for the technical pitching; two 60m ropes are commonly carried both to link pitches efficiently and to make the col rappels on descent.
bivy: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
High bivouacs at the western end of the crest
Crescent Creek Basin camp (below Mt. Terror)

name: Western Dihedral
beta: Pitch 2 is a lieback/stemming crux; pitch 3 is a delicate smearing finger traverse; the upper two pitches ease into pleasant smearing and cruising to the top. Protection mixes hand-drilled bolts on the faces with gear in the dihedral/crack sections.
overview: A 5-pitch, 700-ft moderate slab line up the South Face with two distinct crux pitches sandwiched between easier friction climbing above and below.

current.approach: South Face is the southwest-facing slab wall around the corner west of the Illusion Wall, with its own approach separate from Waterfall Basin. Take I-5 to the Arlington exit, SR 530 east through Oso to Darrington, then Squire Creek Road to the washout-blocked parking area. Walk the old roadbed past the flagged landslide crossing to the brown Squire Creek Trail #654 sign and 8-10 minutes beyond it, to two cut logs either side of the road with old logging cable visible. Turn right a few steps past them on a well-beaten boot track, drop to Squire Creek and ford it where it is shallowest (hard in early season or after storms), then follow the climbers' track briefly downstream before it turns uphill, crosses a tributary and climbs old-growth forest and two gullies, steep and dirty near the top, to the grassy saddle, about 3 hours from the car. For this route go left (west) from the saddle to the base of Skeena26, scramble about 100 m of class 4 ramps and small dihedrals to a large shelf, follow it left to a deep gully (two-bolt anchor for a hand line or a short rappel), cross it and follow a cairned boot track west across talus and cedar ribs to the large talus field below the far western wall, about an hour from Skeena26.
approach_variant_names: Squire Creek trail, cut logs, ford and the grassy saddle
current.descent: Descend by rappelling the line of ascent using the fixed hand-drilled bolt anchors; two 60m ropes recommended.
current.detailed_rack: Single standard rack to 4 inches, about a dozen quickdraws plus a few longer/extended ones, and two 60m ropes for the rappel descent.
current.pro_needs: Protection alternates between hand-drilled 3/8" stainless bolts on the friction/face sections and natural gear (cams/nuts) in the dihedral and crack features; no power-drilled bolts exist here since the route lies within Wilderness.

name: North Ridge
beta: Pick up the climbers' trail from the pullout, cross the basin and gain the notch between Whistler and Cutthroat. Follow the north ridge, which dips slightly in places, to the summit pyramid. There the rock opens into many possible lines; keeping to the north (right-hand) side is easier, and there are rappel slings on the far side. Expect loose rock and choose lines carefully.
overview: The north ridge is the rock route on Whistler, climbed from the highway shoulder shared with Cutthroat Peak. A climbers' trail drops into the open basin between the two peaks, then the route follows the ridge to the summit pyramid, mostly class 3 with some class 4 steps, over about 2,700 ft of gain. The ridge is exposed in places, and a fall would have serious consequences.

current.approach: Park on the wide paved shoulder of SR-20 about three quarters of a mile west of the signed Blue Lake trailhead lot, on the north side, where there is no guard rail. A good climbers' trail leads from the road through forest into the basin. No pass is needed at the pullout; the Blue Lake lot needs a forest pass.
current.descent: Retrace the ridge. A short loose step is usually rappelled instead of downclimbed.

name: South Ridge / Southwest Slope
beta: From a roadside turnout on SR-20 (or alternatively the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead), a boot path climbs through open forest and a meadow basin, then rises on a traversing line to intersect the level part of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. From there the route follows the ridge and adjoining gullies — staying north of a loose gully band and using a visible ramp near the headwall — to the 7,790 ft summit; an alternative continues the ridge to about 6,800 ft before cutting left across gullies onto gentler terrain on the southwest slope for the final push. It is class 3 scrambling throughout, with class 4 moves possible depending on line choice.
overview: A non-technical summit on the Okanogan Range crest between Rainy Pass and Washington Pass, in Chelan County within the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest. Whistler is linked by a high ridge to Cutthroat Peak (8,050 ft), 0.8 mile north-northeast, and offers a broad, mostly-talus scramble popular as an early-season warm-up or a corn-snow ski descent in late spring. The standard route climbs the mountain's south ridge and southwest slope; a steeper alternative ascends a broad gully system visible from Rainy Pass.

current.approach: Two trailheads serve this scramble, both off SR-20 between Rainy Pass and Washington Pass. Option A (PCT approach, most commonly used): park at the marked Pacific Crest Trail North trailhead lot on the north side of Rainy Pass (~4,850 ft, next to the Road 600 turnoff). From the lot, leave the PCT almost immediately and strike out cross-country/climber's-path east into open forest, gaining steeply through timber and over downed logs — there is no maintained tread once you leave the PCT. Continue up through the trees (expect lingering snow patches into early summer) to about 6,100 ft, where the forest opens into a meadow basin below the west ridge/gully complex. From the basin, trend south/southeast on a rising traverse to gain the col/basin between Whistler and the southwest peak of Cutthroat, then work up the broad west ridge or the shallow gully just north of it to the summit shoulder; the final short section involves a rock gully with a visible ramp along the headwall over downsloping slabs and loose gravel — a helmet is recommended here for rockfall from parties above. Round trip via this line runs roughly 3.7 miles with about 3,000 ft of gain (trailhead 4,850 ft to summit 7,790 ft). Option B (highway turnout approach, reaches the true south ridge): from the unmarked pullout on SR-20 about 3.1 miles east of Rainy Pass (0.7 mile before the Blue Lake trailhead, ~5,000 ft), walk back down/along the road shoulder to a boot path that starts at the west edge of a stand of trees. Follow the boot path up through a meadow, then rising-traverse to intersect the level portion of Whistler's south ridge at about 6,180 ft. From there, scramble up the ridge and connecting gullies to the summit; alternatively leave the ridge around 6,800 ft, cross a couple of gullies left (west) onto gentler southwest-facing slopes, and finish to the summit that way. This line is also about 4 miles round trip with ~3,000 ft gain. Both approaches are trail-less above the first stretch of forest — expect route-finding, loose talus/scree in the gullies, and class 2-3 terrain with occasional class 3-4 moves and real exposure near the ridge crest and summit gully; no reliable water source above the lower forest, so carry what you need from the car. No creek fords or avalanche paths of note on the standard summer line, but early-season snow lingers in the forest and basin and can make the gully sections firm or icy. Crossing over to the stream too high in the forest costs extra bushwhacking; contour at a lower elevation instead.
approach_variant_names: Rainy Pass PCT lot, then cross-country east into the meadow basin and the col toward Cutthroat's southwest peak
The unmarked SR-20 turnout, then a boot path onto the true south ridge at 6,180 ft
current.descent: There is no rappelling on this route — it's a walk-off/downclimb, reversing whichever line was used on the way up. From the summit, downclimb the summit gully (loose gravel and downsloping slabs — take care with rockfall for anyone below) back to the shoulder, then descend either the west ridge/gully back into the meadow basin and forest (Option A) or drop onto the south ridge and retrace the rising traverse back to the meadow and boot path to the highway turnout (Option B). Loose rock and talus in the gullies is the main descent hazard — down-climb facing in on the steeper class 3 sections and stay alert for parties below. Some ski mountaineers descend a separate snow-filled west gully (~35°, over 1,000 ft of sustained fall-line terrain funneling to a waterfall lower down, requiring an exit right into the glades to avoid the falls) as a spring ski descent, but that is a snow-season variant, not part of the standard summer scramble descent, and should not be used as a hiking descent once snow is out. rappels: 0.
current.detailed_rack: No roped protection is used on the standard scramble route.
current.pro_needs: None — this is an unroped Class 3 scramble with no fixed protection or technical rack; a rope and basic protection could be carried by conservative parties for the class 4 variations, but are not standard.
current.rope_note: Non-technical: boot path from SR-20 near Rainy Pass up through meadows to the south ridge (6180ft), then ridge/gully scrambling to the summit. No roped climbing required.

name: White Mountain Scramble
beta: This is a remote, non-technical scramble whose difficulty is really the approach: roughly 15-17 miles of biking/hiking one-way just to reach camp near Anderson Pass, followed by an 8-mile round-trip, ~4,000 ft scramble day with no maintained trail above the pass. The summit push itself is rated Class 2. There is no record of a notable first ascent or established named line — it is climbed as a cross-country objective, not a route in the rock-climbing sense.
overview: White Mountain (6,378 ft) sits in the remote southern interior of Olympic National Park, 0.95 mi southwest of its higher neighbor Mount La Crosse (6,417 ft), with an unnamed glacier occupying the north cirque between the two summits. It rises above the headwaters of the Duckabush and West Fork Dosewallips rivers near O'Neil Pass, Anderson Pass, and LaCrosse Pass. There is no maintained trail to the summit; parties reach it via a long wilderness approach (2-4 days round trip for most parties) followed by an off-trail Class 2 scramble on talus, heather benches, and open subalpine forest.

current.approach: Dosewallips approach (north): from the vehicle road end on the Dosewallips Road (about 8.5 mi from US-101), hike or bike the closed roadbed ~6.5-7 mi (~1,900 ft gain) to the former Dosewallips Ranger Station, then continue on the West Fork Dosewallips Trail to Honeymoon Meadows camp (about 14 miles from the road end, established campsite). Total approach gain to camp is roughly 5,300 ft. Duckabush approach (south/west): from the Duckabush River trailhead (Brinnon, drivable year-round, no washout), hike the Duckabush River Trail 6.2 mi to the park boundary and on toward O'Neil Pass (16.1 mi park-boundary-to-pass), camping at Marmot Lake (established site, toilet, bear wire), or continuing up past Hart Lake to Lake La Crosse in the basin directly below the peak.
approach_variant_names: West Fork Dosewallips to Anderson Pass
current.descent: Standard descent is to reverse the ascent scramble route back to camp (Honeymoon Meadows or Marmot Lake depending on approach). There is no established rappel or technical descent; the main concerns are loose talus/scree on the upper slopes and losing the line back to camp in open forest/heather terrain with no marked path - note landmarks or track your ascent on the way up.
current.detailed_rack: No technical climbing gear is required; the standard route is Class 2 scrambling on talus, heather, and open slopes with no reported pitched climbing or fixed protection.
bivy: Lake LaCrosse and Hart Lake — the base for Mount La Crosse and White Mountain
current.rope_note: No rope needed: the standard line is a non-technical Class 2 scramble on talus, heather and open slopes south of Anderson Pass.

name: Northwest Shoulder
beta:
Begin on Niederprum Trail #953/653, which quickly degenerates into a steep, brushy boot path climbing to an alpine bench near the old Niederprum mine. Continue on snow to Lone Tree Pass (~4,900 ft; the 'lone tree' is actually a cluster of three trees, not at the pass), traverse below the northwest ridge to High Pass (~6,000-6,030 ft), cross onto the Whitehorse Glacier, and climb a snow/ice ridge to the base of the summit block, finishing with exposed Class 3 scrambling to the true summit.

Early in the season, roughly April to June, the same line is climbed as a continuous snow and ice route. Parties stay on snow higher on the shoulder and face instead of threading the rock bands that appear later, keep climber's right on the glacier to avoid the worst crevassing, and meet a steep, sometimes icy rollover of about 50-55 degrees, the crux in these conditions. It is a popular ski and splitboard objective: many skin or boot the glacier basin and switch to crampons only for the final steep pitch below the summit, then ski back toward High Pass and Lone Tree Pass. Once deep snow has buried the brush, some parties go more directly up Snow Gulch from near the trailhead and stash skis around 2,500 ft for the descent.
overview: Rises dramatically above Darrington with one of the largest vertical reliefs in the Cascades — the north face gains about 6,000 ft in under 2 miles. Standard mountaineering line: a difficult, brushy trail hike up to Lone Tree Pass and High Pass, a crossing of the small So-Bahli-Ahli (Whitehorse) Glacier, and a short, exposed Class 3-4 scramble on the summit rock. Nels Bruseth made the first recorded ascent in 1909.

current.approach: Drive Old Mine Road to its dead end at a steel gate (about 540 ft); the Niederprum Trailhead (Trail #653, ~918 ft) is about 1.25 miles farther up the old road on foot. Because the Moose Creek bridge just past the gate has been closed and barricaded with boulders for years, you now park at the gate, scramble over the boulder barricade, and cross the old wooden bridge on foot to rejoin the road to the actual trailhead about 1.25 miles farther on — this detour adds roughly 2.6 miles round trip and 400 ft of extra gain beyond what older published mileages state. From the signed trailhead, Trail #653 switchbacks up through forest for about 1.3 miles, crossing into Boulder River Wilderness (marked by a small boundary sign) and passing an old slide-alder opening with views north to Darrington and the Sauk Valley. At roughly 3,200 ft you reach 'the flat,' a level clearing that was the site of Chas Niederprum's old mining cabin — a natural rest/camp spot with good views of the peak. Beyond the flat the maintained tread ends; continue on a climbers' boot path through thinning, brushy forest (deadfall to weave around) up to continuous snow around 2,600 ft of gain from the trailhead. From there make a gently rising traverse south for about 0.5 mile into a wide, usually snow-filled couloir (holds snow into early July in normal years); ascend it to Lone Tree Pass (~4,970–5,000 ft, roughly 2 miles and 4,000+ ft above the trailhead — despite the name there are three trees near the pass, not one). From the pass, do a pleasant ridge traverse east for 600–700 m, then drop southeast through trees to a bench near a small lake/flat meadow (a sheltered, view-blessed bivy option). Continue a long rising traverse east for roughly 2 km through forest and open slopes below cliff bands, then climb a gully/open slope to High Pass (~6,032–6,100 ft). Cross High Pass onto the So-Bahli-Ahli (Whitehorse) Glacier and continue up snow (up to ~35° at the steepest) toward the summit snow ridge; rope up for crevasse hazard, which becomes real from roughly July onward. Key hazards along the way: the barricaded creek/bridge crossing at the start, avalanche-prone terrain in the entry couloir to Lone Tree Pass, vague/brushy route-finding beyond 'the flat,' crevasses on the upper glacier in mid-to-late season, and the summit bergschrund/moat, which by midsummer often forces a short section of 5th-class rock or a delicate roped snow-bridge crossing just below the top. No reliable water past the trailhead area once you're on snow — carry what you need or plan to melt.
approach_variant_names: Niederprum Trail #653 to Lone Tree Pass and High Pass
Snow Gulch direct (deep snow only)
current.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line. From the true summit, downclimb the steep upper snow/ice slope below the top (up to about 60°, and often icy rather than soft by afternoon) back down to the bergschrund/moat that guards the summit block. Most parties make one rappel here to bypass the schrund rather than downclimb through it — anchor options are natural: slung webbing around a rock horn/chockstone, or an old fixed piton left by previous parties (treat any in-place tat or pins as suspect; one recent trip report had a piton fail under load, so back it up or build your own gear anchor in the rock). A doubled 30 m rope (or a single 60 m rope doubled) is generally sufficient to clear the gap; in lean/late-season years when the schrund has opened wider, some parties report needing two rappels or a longer single line. Early in the season, when the moat is well snow-bridged, this step can sometimes be downclimbed with a boot-axe belay instead. Below the schrund, re-cross the glacier, downclimb (or glissade, snow conditions permitting) back through the connecting slopes to High Pass, reverse the long traverse to Lone Tree Pass, then descend the entry couloir — a fast glissade or boot-ski in soft afternoon snow, a careful plunge-step descent if firm — back to treeline and the Niederprum Trail. From there it's a straightforward hike out to the trailhead and the Moose Creek bridge/boulder-barricade crossing. This is a long day: parties commonly report 12–14 hours car-to-car, so plan for an early alpine start and be off the upper glacier and past the couloir before afternoon warming increases rockfall/wet-slide risk.
current.detailed_rack: Glacier travel gear and rope; light protection for the Class 3 summit scramble.
current.pro_needs: Mostly snow/glacier; minimal rock pro.
